source.title: Towards a Learning Theory of Representation Alignment
source.authors: Francesco Insulla; Shuo Huang; Lorenzo Rosasco

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical results relating representation alignment to the performance of stitched models. It tests the interchangeability-by-stitching version under stated assumptions, using mathematical bounds rather than empirical model comparisons.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical results about stitching error and alignment. Its discussion of scale-related empirical findings cites other work; those cited results are not rows here. It reports no experiments on trained models.
record.test_reason: A purely theoretical paper with no experiments on trained models. It unifies alignment metrics (KA, CKA, HSIC, distance alignment, MI) and proves conditional bounds linking stitching risk to an alignment quantity. None of its results show whether real models' representations converge or can be swapped with little loss. The bounds say stitching error is small if alignment is high, but never establish that alignment is high, so they cannot bear on whether V4 or any other version holds. Huh et al. and Bansal et al. are cited as motivation only.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors review and unify alignment metrics (kernel alignment, distance alignment, independence testing) and formalize stitching. They derive bounds on stitching error from misalignment, calling this a first step toward a learning theory of representation alignment. They also claim that linking kernel alignment to stitching supports building universal cross-modal models as scale grows. That claim rests on Huh et al.'s cited experiments, not on their own data.
record.recipe_differences: This is a theoretical treatment of kernel, distance, and other alignment notions, with derived stitching-risk bounds; it does not reproduce the original empirical scale or cross-modal measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The theoretical guarantees depend on assumptions including linear stitching, decoder Lipschitzness or linearity, task-risk conditions, and function-class inclusion. The paper notes that the bound's alignment quantity Ã2 differs from standard kernel alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Theorem 1 shows linear stitching risk is at most model 2's risk plus terms in a misalignment quantity Ã2, for a Lipschitz decoder. Remark 5 adds that alignment implies stitching similarity but not the converse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theory: representation (kernel-type) alignment upper-bounds excess linear stitching risk, making alignment a stronger similarity notion than stitchability.

fits_no_version.finding: Lemma 2: with linear output decoders and d ≤ d2, minimum linear stitching risk equals model 1's own risk, regardless of the representations' similarity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theory: stitching into a linear head measures only the difference in model risk, not representational similarity.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 3 proves several metric links: CKA is normalized HSIC; distance alignment equals 8C(1−KA) under unit-norm features; and MI and Wasserstein independence measures are functions of the cross-covariance spectrum.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Theory: common representational similarity metrics are related through the cross-covariance spectrum, with kernel alignment as the central quantity.

record.problems: No empirical evaluation of trained models is reported. The stitching guarantees rely on simplifying assumptions, and the bound does not establish that its alignment-dependent terms are small in practice.

untested.parts: All: no scale or capability sweep and no model comparisons.
All empirically: no stitching, linear mapping, relative representations or unpaired mapping is performed on real models. Only conditional bounds relating stitching risk to alignment are derived.
All: no feature or circuit analysis.
Not tested empirically. The paper relates metrics mathematically and notes Ã2 differs from kernel alignment, but does not vary metrics, settings or inputs on models.
All: no plateau or shared-data analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with V4 supports/limits_scope labels should be dropped. Conditional theorems about abstract representations give no evidence on whether trained models' representations align or are interchangeable. Lemma 2 in particular holds by construction for any representations, so it cannot support V4. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No scale or capability sweep, nor comparison of independently trained models with different architectures, objectives, or data.
No empirical comparison of image and caption representations as vision and language model performance changes.
No comparison of same-architecture networks trained from different initializations or analysis of shared features or subspaces.

The results concern stitching under mathematical assumptions, not empirical tests of learned models. Relative representations, stitching across specific trained layers, and mappings without paired data are not tested.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
The paper relates several alignment definitions mathematically but does not test whether convergence findings vary with metric settings or inputs, or disappear out of distribution.
No empirical test of convergence plateaus, shared-data explanations, or shared-objective explanations.

rows.subject: two representations f1 and f2
rows.operation_detail: Shows that the minimum linear stitching risk equals the risk of model 1 under the lemma's assumptions.
rows.note: The paper says this setting includes models whose output layer is linear, and RKHS models with a linear map of representations.
rows.check: Lemma 2 is a mathematical identity: with linear decoders, minimum linear stitching risk equals model 1's risk. It holds by construction for any representations with d ≤ d2. It shows the stitching measure is uninformative in that case, not that trained models' representations are interchangeable. It should not be 'observed' for V4.
